speechtext:
1.	How many lawyers, by provinces, have been engaged by the Department of National Revenue, during each of the last five years, to write letters or take other steps in connection with the collection of sales taxes?
2.	How much has been collected as the result of such efforts?
3.	What is the total amount paid to such lawyers, by provinces, during each of the past five years, for such services?
4.	Why does the Department of National Revenue not write such letters and do such work itself?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I should like to answer this question orally. I have endeavoured to assemble the information sought in this question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but find it entails more work, I am sure, than the member could have anticipated.
Questions
Our records reveal that, for the five years referred to, a total of 703 different lawyers were used in sales tax cases. To break down the figures as requested raises the problem of first segregating sales tax cases from excise tax cases, a practically impossible task, since these cases are not separated in the records, and in many instances both forms of tax are involved.
I should like the hon. member to know, too, that since 1952 legal agents have only been appointed for the prosecution of delinquents, and not for the collection of taxes, as implied in the question. Our departmental officers carry on collection proceedings until legal action by way of prosecution becomes necessary. It would be a task of several months to even approximate the over-all results of the action taken by legal agents, since in many cases the threat of prosecution results in the payment of both arrears and current taxes, whereas in the case of prosecution less than the amount may be collected and, in some instances, imprisonment imposed as an alternative to failure to pay the fines and the taxes.
The dimensions of this problem can be indicated by the fact that some 2,500 separate cases were handled by the 703 lawyers employed during this period. Should the member have a more specific inquiry in this case, I will be pleased to see if we can answer it.

2.	In this area how many applications for citizenship were awaiting hearing on November 30 and December 31, 1954, and on January 31, 1955?
3.	In this area how many applications were heard in each of these months?
4.	How many judges conduct such hearings?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had a word with the hon. gentleman who is asking this question and I explained to him that the information asked for in parts 2, 3 and 4 of the question would be information in the possession of the courts, which are of course under provincial jurisdiction. While I have no doubt that there would be the greatest co-operation in supplying it, it would be asking for something that is not normally within our federal records. We could provide the answer to part 5. The answer to the first part is, of course, York county.
However, I rose to say something else about this situation which I think is what the hon. gentleman is really trying to get at. The

situation in York county is very unsatisfactory indeed. About one-fifth of the immigrants who have come to Canada since the war, as nearly as we have been able to calculate, have settled in the Toronto area. Time has gone on and the number of applications for citizenship that we anticipate this year is far beyond the capacity of the courts under present arrangements to carry out in a satisfactory manner.
I have been in touch with the attorney general of Ontario, with the judges and with the clerk of the court, all of whom have been most co-operative. I visited the premises myself and the Minister of Public Works has since made new space available. We are trying as fast as we can to make new arrangements which will make it possible to deal expeditiously with these citizenship applications, as I am sure every hon. member would vant them to be dealt with.

In view of the explanation and the recognition of the problem in the Toronto area in connection with processing applications for certificates of citizenship, which was really the point of my question, and in view of the assurance given to the house by the minister that he recognizes this problem and proposes to deal with it, I am prepared to drop parts 2, 3 and 4 of the question. I would be glad to have an answer to part 5. Part 1 has been answered. My main purpose in asking the question was to have it recognized that there is a serious backlog in dealing with the processing of applications for citizenship in Toronto.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: One of the questions has been answered. Paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 have been dropped, and paragraph 5 will stand.

I see that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is in his seat. I believe that he himself should consider this problem carefully and introduce legislation which will restore to the family allowance cheque the purchasing power it had when the cheques were first issued back in 1945.
I would go even further and say that no more should this government, than any other government, rest content with the body of social security legislation as it now stands.

Family Allowances Act Not only should it at this time restore the value of the family allowance but its objective should be to increase the value of the family allowance in the years to come. A nation cannot stand still. I do not think any government should allow its social security program to stand still or worse-as it is doing with the family allowance-allow the benefit of family allowance gradually to wither away as the result of inflation.
A year ago my motion asked in specific terms that the value of the family allowance be restored to the value it had when the act was first brought into effect in 1944. I have deliberately worded this motion in more general terms. It sets forth a principle, namely that the family allowance should be increased. I challenge the government to allow a vote this afternoon on the principle of this motion. Every year that I moved this motion I have said that I was not endeavouring to take away any credit that was due the former prime minister, the late W. L. Mackenzie King, and that I was not attempting to take away any credit that was due the government. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) amended that statement by saying that J. S. Woods-worth, the late leader of this party, also played a substantial part over the years in promoting social security legislation. But this government that has followed the Mackenzie King government should not allow the benefits of the family allowance legislation to wither away through lack of action and because it has failed to restore the purchasing power of the family allowance.
The family allowance is one of the most important social security measures on the statute books in Canada. Recent figures show that family allowance payments are now made to over two million families. The number of children on whose behalf family allowance payments are made was 4,729,000 in March, 1953. Family allowance payments for the year ended March 31, 1953, amounted to $334 million.
The government may argue that, with increasing population, the amount paid out for family allowance at current rates has increased and that that is sufficient burden on the nation. However, I should like to point out that in 1946-47 family allowances were 

paid to the amount of $245 million out of a gross national product of $12 billion, so that the ratio of the family allowance to the gross national product at that time was approximately 2 per cent. If the same ratio were maintained today there should be paid out in family allowances not less than $480 million. However, the amount paid out in the year ended March 31, 1953, was $334 million. Not only in relationship to the purchasing power of the family allowance cheque but in the relationship of the amount paid out in family allowances to the gross national product-the wealth production of this country-the government is allowing family allowances to decrease as the years go by.
I believe that family allowances have been of great value in helping parents to feed their children better. I believe that family allowances have increased nutritional standards. I believe that family allowance cheques have enabled parents to clothe their children better. There is no doubt in my mind that the family allowance cheques have enabled parents to have their children receive a better education. There is no doubt in my mind that the payment of the family allowance has meant better medical care for the children of this country. I am one who believes that our nation's greatest asset is its children. If we want to build a nation that is secure for the future, we need now to look after the welfare of the children of family allowance age. Because I believe this, I have once again moved this motion asking that family allowances be increased.
The general consumer price index since 1945 has increased considerably. From 1945 to 1954 there has been an increase in the index from 75 to 116-2, or an increase of some 55 per ce-nt. The two main items on which I would think the family allowance cheque is ordinarily spent, namely food and clothing, have increased by an even larger amount. In 1945 the index for food was 66-3. In 1954 it had become 112-2, or an increase of 69 per cent. Let us look at the index for clothing in the same period. In 1945 the index stood at 66-9; in 1954 it stood at 109-4, an increase of 63-5 per cent. While the general cost of living index has increased, the cost of the main items for which the family allowance cheque is spent has increased at an even greater rate. I suggest that that is an additional reason why this government should take action at this time to increase payments made under the family allowance.
The government has not hesitated to increase the salaries of public servants and especially to increase by large amounts salaries of public servants who are already receiving relatively high salaries. Almost

every income group in the nation in the last
10	years has received substantial increases in salaries and income. That being the case, I believe the government should consider an increase in the family allowance.
As I have already said, my greatest objection to inaction is the fact that the government stands idly by while the purchasing power of the family allowance cheque has gone down and down. In this house the other day I mentioned something of a similar attitude on the part of this government in relation to another security measure, namely prairie farm assistance. The government had allowed the value of the moneys paid out under that act to decrease, I believe, by some 58 per cent during the period in which it has been in effect. This government has allowed the value or the purchasing power of the old age pension cheque to go down by a substantial amount since the last increase in the monthly cheque for old age pensioners, namely April, 1949, until today the $40 a month for the old age pension is nothing short of a starvation allowance. No old age pensioner in Canada can live in decency on $40 a month if that pensioner has no other income. The same callous attitude is shown with regard to family allowances.
Is "callous" the word?

Exactly. The $5 a month family allowance cheque, in the first year after the government had made its initial payment, was reduced in value by 10 cents. It took only one year for the government to reach in and take away 10 cents of the value of a $5 family allowance cheque. The next year the same government stepped in and, by allowing inflation to run wild and doing nothing to maintain the value of the family allowance cheque, allowed another 50 cents to be taken away from that cheque. So that after two years the cheque had become worth just $4.40 in terms of 1945 purchasing power. In the next year the government allowed 50 cents to be taken away from the family allowance cheque and it became worth $3.90.
All of these calculations are based on changes in the consumer price index, the official index of the dominion bureau of statistics. In 1949 another 15 cents was taken from the family allowance cheque and it became worth just $3.75. In 1950 another
11	cents was taken from the cheque and in purchasing power it became worth $3.64. In 1951 a further 35 cents was taken from the family allowance cheque and it became worth just $3.29 in terms of 1945 purchasing power. In 1952, with another increase in the cost of living, the value of the family allowance cheque went down an additional
Family Allowances Act 8 cents and it became worth only $3.21. In
1953	there was a lowering of the consumer price index as the result of which 3 cents was restored to the value of the family allowance cheque, making it worth $3.24. In
1954	the value of the family allowance cheque again decreased by 2 cents and it was worth only $3.22 based on the purchasing power of 1945 dollars. The government had allowed a reduction of $1.78 to take place since 1945 in the value of the $5 family allowance cheques.
I think that demonstrates how necessary it is for the government to do something towards restoring the value of the family allowance. Of course what has happened to family allowance payments in other categories is similar. In the same period the $6 cheque was reduced in value by $2.13, becoming worth only $3.87. The value of the $7 monthly family allowance cheque has gone down by $2.48 to $4.52. The value of the $8 family allowance cheque has gone down by $2.84 until, in terms of 1945 purchasing power and according to the consumer price index, it is only worth $5.16.
That means, Mr. Speaker, that almost year by year the value of family allowance has gone down and has been allowed to wither away. The effect on families must be very serious indeed. Oh, members of parliament who are living quite comfortably, whose income in this period has been increased very substantially indeed, almost doubled, may not realize just how little income a very large percentage of Canadians actually obtain. The 1951 census shows that of 4,085,000 workers 2,188,000, or 53-5 per cent, earned less than $2,000 a year. In 1951 over half the wage earners in Canada were earning less than $2,000 a year.
It is no doubt true that since 1951 wages have gone up to some extent, but I am sure if statistics were available today they would show that a large percentage of Canadian workers earn a very small salary indeed. The 1951 figures show that 1,497,000 wage earners, or 37 per cent, earned less than $1,500, and that 895,000, or 22 per cent, earned less than $1,000 a year. When one considers these figures in conjunction with the statement made in the house by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that 19 per cent of the working population are responsible for 84 per cent of the children, one can see that the average income of the people of Canada who have children is not high. In fact it is low, and with such a low income as these statistics indicate I believe there is no excuse whatever for the government not taking action immediately to restore the value of family allowance cheques. And

Family Allowances Act why? So that Canadian children can be better fed, better clothed, better housed, better educated and have the opportunity of obtaining better medical assistance.
In speaking on this question on former occasions the Minister of National Health and Welfare has to my mind advanced only one argument against increasing family allowances. His argument can be summed up in these words: Where is the money going to come from? The motion is fine, says the minister, but if the member moving the motion were on the government side of the house he would then be responsible to the Canadian public and would have to find where he could get the money.
The statement has been made in debate after debate that such a move would necessarily add to the terrible tax burden on the Canadian people. The present Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) has answered that argument very successfully in the past when he has pointed out that family allowance payments are not a burden in the ordinary sense of the tax burden, in the sense of the burden of national defence expenditures, that they are not a deadweight burden on the Canadian public but rather that they are merely transfer payments. In the general tax structure of Canada family allowances ordinarily mean that the well-to-do paying most of the taxes help to take care of the children of parents who have smaller incomes.
When one considers that payments for family allowance are merely transfer payments, I say that even if our tax structure today were as high as the Canadian public could bear we could afford higher family allowances because it would be a transfer and a transfer only. But I believe that under present economic conditions the government could increase family allowances and restore their value without adding to the tax burden of the Canadian public in any way, shape or form.
Tell us how.

To point out how it can be done, I have in my hand the estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1956, and I see that a reduction in estimates of $153 million is being forecast. There is $153 million. That in itself would be almost sufficient to restore the family allowances to their value in terms of 1945 dollars. I suggest to the government that rather than considering a reduction in corporation taxes or a reduction in income taxes of the high income tax groups, the government should take the $153 million that it has been estimated will be saved and use it to restore

the value of family allowances. That would not result in any increase in taxes whatsoever.
If the government wants more revenue they should go back and read their 1945 proposals to the provinces at the dominion-provincial conference. If the government would reread those proposals and, having become imbued, if possible, with the same philosophy contained in them, would decide that Canada should no longer suffer from an unemployment situation where there are in the country 600,000 idle persons who should be adding to the wealth of production, if they would apply and practise the philosophy of full employment and do everything possible to see that there was full employment, tax revenues would go away up.
Canada can afford whatever can be produced in Canada. When you want to decide what Canada can afford, try to ascertain the total wealth production that Canada is capable of producing. In 1954 this government has allowed wealth production to be $1,200 million less than it would have been had they adopted a full employment policy. The gross national production may go along fairly level in 1954, after having taken out the factor of widespread crop failure, but the gross national production should go up year after year by not less than 5 per cent because of increasing population and improvements in technology and methods of production.
Any time Canada's gross national production remains level we are losing 5 per cent annually. It is estimated that in 1954 we have lost $1,200 million in wealth production. If that wealth production had been coming forward, not only would the general standard of living of the Canadian people be increased but the revenues going into the federal government would have been increased by at least 5 per cent-yes, by more than 5 per cent-because when wealth production goes up it means more money in the hands of those in the higher income tax brackets and the higher corporation tax brackets, and therefore reflects itself in an even larger percentage increase in tax revenues to the government. Had there been full employment in 1954 we should have had an increase of at least 5 per cent or $225 million in our taxation revenues. Add that to the $153 million reduction in estimates, and you have another $378 million from which the government could take all the money that was necessary to increase the family allowances. Even at this late date, in the light of the fact that Canada has lost $1,200 million of wealth production that will never be regained-it is gone and gone forever-if the government decided on a program of full employment and

full production in 1955, then I suggest there could be regained not only the 5 per cent which was lost in 1954 but the additional 5 per cent that should normally accrue in 1955. With a continuing full employment policy, instead of revenues going up in 1955 by an additional 5 per cent they should go up by an additional 10 per cent or about $450 million. If we add that to the $153 million that the government says it is going to save, we have over $600 million from which family allowances could be paid, old age pensions increased, an expanded program of road development in Canada, increased federal grants for education and health, and all those things that the C.C.F. and the people of Canada believe in and desire.
Instead, the government does literally nothing and allows the value of family allowances to wither away, allows the purchasing power of the $40 per month for old age pensions to wither away. Over a period of 10 years, this government has staged a successful attack on the value of family allowances. This government has been instrumental in the destruction of 35 per cent of the value of family allowances, and that is the reason I propose to the house this day that we consider and vote on a proposition which says that the time has arrived when family allowances in this country should be increased.

If the hon. gentleman did it in a debate it would be much better. I wonder whether it is the same thing in my own constituency? I cannot complain that a large number of people write to me about this matter of family allowances. In my county, the people are sound-minded and they know the difference between what is sensible and what is not. They are very much satisfied with what the government does for them in a particular and in a general way and they are much more grateful than the C.C.F. group may ever be. They tell me often to convey their thanks to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. They have good manners. They are ladies and gentlemen. They have very good manners and they appreciate very highly what is done for them. I should like to make a revelation to you. I discovered by pure chance that instructions are sent out from the Montreal offices of l'union des electeurs to those who are called conquerors. These are sillier fellows who go around getting subscriptions to the organ. I don't mean a musical organ, a harmonious organ, I mean the organ of the group.
Mouth organ.

I had the pleasure of putting one of these out of my office, one of these canvassers, conquerors. I suppose they call them conquerors because they conquer subscriptions. It is a very funny thing. One must have a sense of humour to appreciate it. I am sorry that my hon. friends of the Social Credit group who defend the Quebec group have no sense of humour at all, otherwise they would laugh very heartily.
That surely is too bad.

My hon. friend is quite genial, but he does not have enough sense of humour to savour the whole thing.
Here is what they wrote to the conquerors at large. The name is erased on this bulletin which I was fortunate enough to get. They say that he spoke to Mr. Pouliot, the member

for Temiscouata, who was enraged because he had been disturbed at his work. I am supposed to have said that all my constituents who send petitions are people who pay no taxes. The Social Crediters are quite wrong in that because I never said that those who write to me pay no taxes. Most of my correspondence is made up of sensible letters that I get from my constituents. Do you see the idea of these people in Montreal who send false reports to all these conquerors throughout the province in order that they might become a nuisance to members of parliament?
What are you concerned about? What are you worried about in connection with Social Crediters?

I am not worrying at all. I am just exposing their silliness to the house and to the country. I am not concerned about it. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn) is a very genial colleague and I have great regard for him. He is very different from these people; he is not the same type. If one of these canvassers comes to my office again I will take him by the hand and introduce him to the hon. gentleman. I am not concerned about it. I see through their silliness. I do not want people of good faith to be taken advantage of by these cranks and that is why I am exposing their tactics to the house.
We have work to do, first for our constituents and then for the Canadian people at large. I do not see why a crank should be able to come to my office to disturb me in the work I am doing as a member of parliament for my constituents and for the Canadian people at large. That is the first point. What is worse is that some gullible fellows take for granted what is written in these circulars. I pity them; I have compassion for them.
I want to summarize, as I do not intend to take up all the time this afternoon. I want to tell you, as you know, that the Liberal government has done more than any other government in enacting social legislation. I want to tell you that the Canadian people at large are satisfied with what has been done. They realize the prudence and care exercised by the government and they know it would be impossible to increase family allowances without increasing taxation. That is why they are so careful about it.
During the last election I was in a position to state authoritatively that the amount paid for family allowances and old age pensions in my constituency amounted to $2 million a year. That is some amount. Depending upon population, the same is probably true of the
Family Allowances Act constituency of Assiniboia, of the constituency of Lethbridge, and of the constituency of Bow River and many other constituencies. The result is that over $300 million is paid out each year for that purpose. This should receive recognition from the Canadian people and I am sure they will pay no attention to speeches such as the one that has been made here this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I should also like to echo the numerous petitions which have reached me from various parts of my constituency, urging the government to increase family allowances.
Taking into account the present cost of living, which has more than doubled since 1945, the rate of family allowances is no longer such as to answer the original purpose of that legislation. It therefore follows that what we are asking the government to do today is primarily to raise the value of family allowances to the level which had been set by the government itself, back in 1945.
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to discuss the validity of the reasons advanced by those who might ask for allowances in the province of Quebec. Rather I wish to stick to the point, that is, to determine whether or not they are in the interests of the Canadian nation and family.
The depreciation of the value of our currency as a result of the steadily rising cost of living since 1945 has caused the $5 family allowance to be worth, at this time, no more than $3.22. It will therefore be seen that, by granting this request, the government would only be consistent with the principle it had laid down itself in 1945 when the family allowance rate was originally set at $5. I therefore hope this legitimate request will not be ignored too long by the government.
I am not personally in favour of too many social security measures, because they would lead us to socialism. Still, there are some which are indispensable to the balance of our Canadian standard of living. Industry pays wages which take no account of the family status of the worker. No account is taken of the fact that he may be either a married man with heavy obligations or only a bachelor. Wages are paid on the basis of services rendered, and it would be very hard to do otherwise. Therefore, only the govern-

The increase in family allowances is not requested because of unemployment, as it is obvious that family allowances were not intended to replace employment. On various occasions, there has been talk of the need1 for increased immigration to this country, in order to raise the population to 30 million people within a few years. However, Canadian families are denied proper family allowances, geared to the present cost of living, which would allow them to take care in a much more normal way than immigration of the need for increased population, through family growth. Of course, every time this question is raised in this house, the budget argument is put forward, "Where shall we find the money?"
When, for reasons of security, it was considered necessary to devote close to 40 per cent of the budget to defence, no one asked: "Where shall we find the money?" It was said: "It is essential to the security of the country, it has to be done". And it was done.
Yet, when it comes to the family, the very basis of society, the most valuable asset that we as lawmakers should protect, the question is asked: "Where shall we find the money?" True, it is the duty of the representatives of the country to distribute public moneys according to needs, but they should also distribute them according to the scale of values. And in that scale of values what social asset can have precedence over the family? Besides, what is given families by increasing family allowances is perhaps the best investment that the nation could make for its future. Mr. Speaker, it is with some reluctance that I feel obliged to comment on this
Family Allowances Act motion. If a vote should come I feel I must vote against the proposal, even though it was introduced by my friend and colleague, the hon. member for Assiniboia. I should like to make it crystal clear that I support the principle of family allowances, and I am convinced that family allowances are making a real contribution to the well-being of the nation. I hope, moreover, the day will come when we can increase the level of these allowances. However, in my opinion such a proposition is neither realistic nor practicable today.
As I read the estimates, the government is planning to pay out $384 million in family allowances this year, if the rates remain exactly as they are at the present time. That is a lot of money. The resolution which my good friend has proposed today is framed in general language. However, the one he moved some two years ago suggested that the level of allowances should be increased to a point where it would take care of the cost of living increase which has transpired since the original legislation was introduced. If such a proposition were accepted, I believe it would cost the taxpayers of Canada roughly $200 million.
In view of the already very heavy commitments we have for national defence, and in view of the very heavy commitments we have for existing social welfare measures, I think it would be most difficult to find another $200 million at this time. I have read in the newspapers statements by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) that he was going to find it difficult this year to balance his budget. I have seen reports to the effect that he could well have a deficit of about $100 million. It is one thing to propose expenditures of this kind but it is usually quite another to find the money to pay for them.
Perhaps I am wrong, but as I see it before you can give a dollar to one person you first of all have to take that dollar away from someone else. If we have to find another $200 million for family allowances it must come from taxation. What taxes are going to be increased? I listened to my good friend and colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia, but frankly I could not understand his economic reasoning. Perhaps I am not as bright as I should be, but I still could not comprehend his arguments.
I would remind the house that our budget this year is approaching the $5 billion mark. Governments at the three levels are already taking from Canadians 33 cents out of every dollar in the form of taxation. I do not think he wants to see that 33 cents increased. It is easy to say that you can get the revenue needed for a proposition such as this by taxing the rich more severely. But if you study

Family Allowances Act the statistics published by the Department of National Revenue you will find that there are not enough rich people in Canada to yield such revenue.
I would refer hon. members to page 8 of the taxation statistics for 1954. There you will find that the total income of all Canadians who earned $10,000 or more was only slightly over $1 billion. If you confiscated that whole amount you would still only have about 20 per cent of the federal budget. Therefore I submit to the house that we cannot finance measures of this kind simply by taking more money from the rich. I say that if legislation of this kind is passed it should be clearly realized that it is the average Canadian, the labouring man, the farmer, the small businessman and so on, who is going to have to pay for it.
Not at all.
Why not?

Never.

As far as family allowances are concerned, I think we have gone quite a way. As a matter of fact the United States, which is a much richer country than Canada, has not gone nearly as far as we have. Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this resolution. Last year, when there seemed to be some difference of opinion among my hon. friends opposite, I cannot remember ever finding myself on the same side as the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) as opposed to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), but on this occasion I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre is speaking plain common sense, and I am sorry to say that I cannot even find diplomatic words to describe the practicability of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
He knows it.

If the hon. member for Assiniboia is just trying to carry on general propaganda in favour of higher family allowances at some time in the future, then I can assure him that we on this side of the


house are constantly keeping before the government the advantage of having higher benefits for the people who draw family allowances as well as higher benefits for all the other people who draw any kind of benefits under the welfare state set-up that we have in Canada.
When I heard my hon. friend suggest that at this time and as of this very moment it is a practical proposition to increase family allowances without having either an increase in taxation or an increase in the public debt, then I can only say that he knows better. He is too hard-headed a man for that; otherwise he never would have got first-class honours for writing that thesis on wheat about which we heard the other day. I am compelled to say that while I hardly ever agree with my hon. friends to the extreme right, I do believe that the campaign being carried on for higher family allowances by the Quebec section of the Social Credit movement is more honest, because at least the Quebec wing of the Social Credit movement have a proposal attached to their demand for higher family allowances which would purport to show how the government could get the money. The Quebec wing not only say there should be higher family allowances-I think they want to double them-but they advocate doing that by writing direct credits in a cheque book, and of course they say it is just as easy as that.
Perhaps my hon. friends opposite may be able to facilitate the writing in a cheque book process a bit in view of the fact that the de facto minister of finance of British Columbia has now become a director of one of the great chartered banks of Canada. Perhaps they will be able to speed up the process a little bit. If the hon. member for Assiniboia was suggesting as a serious proposition that we could have an increase in family allowances in 1955, when he knows quite well that this parliament is facing a deficit in the present year's budget, then I think he is just not talking common sense.
I see that over in France, at the very time when it has taken about three weeks to find a man who is even willing to try to form a new government in that country which has such great difficulty in keeping its governments for more than two or three months, the man who is drawing the largest crowds is not a very great speaker. He is drawing crowds of about 20,000 people, and has a very popular and very simple program. It can all be summed up in four words: Down with all taxes. He does not believe in paying taxes

of any kind. But I must say that my hon. friend seems to be even more ingenious than this gentleman who is causing such a stir in some parts of France, because the hon. member for Assiniboia says:	Up with family
allowances and down with all taxes.
When I listened to his rather ingenious suggestion as to how we could pay for this increase in family allowances this year without any increase in taxation or without any increase in public debt, it seemed to me he was saying that we could pay for this increase by somehow, in reverse or in retrospect, bringing into being all the production and distribution we did not have. It seems to me something like finding the little man who is not there. My hon. friend talks about inflation in this country. I have sometimes heard criticism of the expenditures this country makes, for instance, in putting a floor under butter to hold up the price. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, every year now, for four years, the hon. member for Assiniboia has brought forward a resolution asking that consideration be given to an increase in family allowances. Certainly one advantage of this practice is that it affords members of the government an opportunity to make a report on one of the major social measures in our country. I think that is essential, because while some hon. members may feel that from time to time there should be improvements in various social measures, including this one, there is a considerable body of opinion in the country, as I well know, which feels that the expenditures by the government of Canada on health and welfare at this time are beyond the capacity of the nation.
Therefore I welcome this opportunity of dealing with this question in its broadest aspects. The hon. member today, as on other occasions, has said that this government was to be congratulated upon bringing in family allowances. I want to say to him that when 'die next provincial election takes place in Saskatchewan I hope he will be among the first to deny suggestions by certain individuals in the provincial government who take credit for this legislation, as though it were a provincial enactment.
To whom are you referring?
The same is true in other provinces, particularly in Quebec.
Would the minister permit a question? To whom are you referring?

To the premier of Saskatchewan.
The experience of the last 10 years- and we have now had family allowances for 10 years-according to a number of special surveys, reports and studies carried out by universities and other disinterested observers, indicates that family allowances have succeeded in accomplishing the objectives for which they were established.
We find that school authorities in the various provinces, especially in Ontario and Nova Scotia, report consistently that family allowances have improved school attendance and reduced truancy and illegal absence from school. Reports from at least a dozen universities and other surveys show the following order of priority in the use of family allowance funds: 1, clothing; 2, food; 3, savings and insurance; 4, education; 5, health and medical care and 6, recreation. And of course authorities dealing with Canada's Indian and Eskimo populations report a notable improvement in the economic health and social status of these families, attributable in a significant degree to this particular measure.
I have here the firsthand opinion of a distinguished senator in the United States, the junior senator for Oregon, who is proposing to urge in the congress of the United States that a measure of this kind be adopted. The senator has spoken in the highest terms of the Canadian family allowances program.
I know of no social measure more responsibly administered and within the concept of our desire to preserve freedom that brings as much social benefit as family allowances. It does not deny the character of a free country, but it does provide, as I say, in a responsible and effective way for those in need of assistance more than any other social measure that I know of to be found in any jurisdiction in any country of the world. *
And so we may feel that the achievements of this measure, introduced as my hon. friend has said by a government of Liberal persuasion, and adopted by practically all members of the house, and now by all parties, indicate that it is a measure, despite criticism from certain quarters, of which we have every reason to be proud.
Now I think we should give careful examination to the resolution before the house. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide an increase in the family allowance.
Last year my hon. friend had a resolution in more precise terms; and likewise the resolutions of the previous two years were

in more precise terms. In one of those resolutions my hon. friend suggested a 60 per cent increase in family allowance payments. In another resolution he suggested that the family allowance payments should be linked with the uncertain fluctuations of the cost of living index.
I never did either one.

The total national expenditures of the provinces and dominion were $1,600 million, but of this $4,847 million of total governmental expenditures our share for social welfare and health was some $1,200 million.
