Family Allowances Act In other words, Mr. Speaker, health and welfare expenditures accounted for nearly 25 cents out of every dollar spent by the federal government last year, and of every dollar spent on health and welfare, family allowances accounted for 29 cents. Therefore anyone who rises in his place and uses the word "callous" in respect of the government, under these circumstances, I am sure either has not had drilled into his mind the importance of these figures or-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Turn around.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
-he has failed to use the kind of language which in the context of a debate like this every hon. member should be prepared to employ. No one in this house is callous to human misery and suffering. Every hon. member in this house is as interested as any other hon. member in doing what should be done to improve the lot of fellow Canadians in the field of health and welfare. It was for that reason that I did not take strong exception to, but I did resent, the suggestion that the government was callous in this and in other similar measures.
I venture to offer the advice that the use of that adjective has not furthered my hon. friend's argument one iota. Last year family allowances accounted for 7.2 per cent of the entire federal budget. My hon. friend said that we are callous, or that we are not interested in the children of this country. Although he said in the first instance, of course, that we were the authors of this plan, he failed to point out that Canada devotes a higher percentage of its social security budget to family allowances than it does to any other program.
Four and a half months from now, namely on July 1, 1955, we shall mark the completion of 10 years of family allowances in this country. When cheques go out for June to families all across the country we shall have passed the $3 billion mark in family allowance payments since the inception of this program. That is hardly a form of callousness on the part of the government or on the part of the people of Canada who make this program possible; for we must not forget that it is out of the hard-earned money of the people of this country that everything we spend in this house is provided.
These payments will reach 2,200,000 Canadian homes every month. They will be paid for the benefit of 5,100,000 children every month. They cost the Canadian taxpayers $1 million a day. By the time a child reaches 16 in Canada, under our plan he has received an amount of $1,188 in family allowances. That is a significant contribution. It is the kind of fact that my hon. friend could have mentioned when he was trying to make a case
IMr. Martin.]

for our acceptance, or our consideration, of the vague proposal that is before you at this time, Mr. Speaker.
In reaching out to parents and children in Canada this program alone benefits at least 50 per cent of the total population of every constituency in Canada. I can say that no program in all our history compares with it in the universal scope of its provisions. No program touches so many of the homes, the families and the children of this nation. It is only because we want to continue this measure and other measures that we have to weigh every proposal for an increase in expenditure with the greatest of care in this house.
My hon. friend could possibly have supported his argument, or strengthened it, by telling us about family allowances in other countries. He could have told us what they were paying in family allowances in New Zealand and Australia. But no; he just made a wide-and I may say an irresponsible assertion without giving any argument-and I say this in the kindliest way-that could be characterized as having much substance, as one would expect from the mature gentleman I know the hon. member really to be.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Smile, Paul, smile.

Let us examine the situation in other countries. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is howling now. He rises in his place here day after day criticizing and endeavouring to pull me to pieces. But when I tell him that others are as interested as he is he cannot stand it, and his quality of impatience bursts forth to interrupt even the speech of a mild-mannered gentleman like the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I want you to prove it.

Let us examine what the annual average payments are in other countries. The average annual payment per child in Canada is $72.48 a year. The next highest is New Zealand, at $70.98; Australia, $57.20; the United Kingdom, $56.44; Sweden, $54.89; and Norway, $32.88. I mention these countries because they are comparable.
Another method of comparison is to take the total expenditure on these programs in relation to net national income. By using that test it will be found that in terms of net national income Canada's contribution to family allowances is almost two and a half times that of Great Britain and well ahead of Australia. Therefore when my hon. friends talk about the callousness of the government, why do they not remind the house and the country that this country, this government,

and this parliament have taken a step which no other country in the world has emulated?
I would remind my hon. friend that at the present time all political parties in this house support this measure. There has been only one note of criticism about the measure in the past five years, and that came from a member of my hon. friend's own party, who arrived at his view based on his concept of what his responsibility and judgment in the matter should be. But I do not want my hon. friend to suggest that anyone on this side, or in any other part of the house, except the hon. gentleman to whom I have referred, is not as fervent in advocacy of family allowances as my hon. friend. As a matter of fact I want to tell my hon. friend that there was much truth in what the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) said today.
All true.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Everything he said was true. To my mind my hon. friend more than any other hon. member of this house comes close to supporting the attitude of Turnon des electeurs. The leader of the Social Credit party has dissociated himself from l'union des electeurs, and so have the other members of that party in this house. I am sure the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) does not regard the proposal, if it can be so called, of the hon. member as one really worthy of consideration at this time, in the light of expanding social measures and the other obligations facing this country. I am sure that if he had the opportunity the hon. member for Peace River would be the first to agree with what I am saying now.
My hon. friend the hon. member for Assiniboia, the author of this new splinter group in the C.C.F. party, has really in one particular allied himself with Turnon des electeurs. I think it is important that this house should know what that group is advocating. I heard a delegation of l'union des electeurs this morning, and they urged me to recommend to this house that we double family allowances. I told them that it could not be done. I gave them the same reasons I am giving now to the house, and other reasons I shall give before I sit down.
They have been circulating many petitions around the country. Here is one addressed to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), and I shall read it in French:
(Translation):
I cannot believe that the members of parliament will resist the great pressure of the whole of the population and will not prevail upon the government to double at this session the rate of family allowances.
Family Allowances Act
(Text):
And listen to this:
(Translation):
One must be very much blinded by war propaganda to sincerely believe that a country needs so much money for war production, when not at war, and can be so stingy toward families raising children. Our ancestors did not do so much for war.
(Text):
Why should we spend money in preparation for defence when there is no war? That is what this petition says. Let us not spend any money fighting communism, for the preservation of decency and freedom; instead let us double family allowances. Here is another one:
(Translation):
The government could very well take the money for these allowances out of its large war budget. There would be no need for an increase in taxation of even one cent for allowances. Families are more in need of bread than of guns to raise children.
(Text):
They say the people of Canada do not need a large budget for the purpose of carrying on war or defence preparations. My hon. friend and everybody in this house knows, and it is our duty to tell these people in every corner of our constituencies, that the only reason we are spending so much money in the building up of our defences is that this is the only way of preserving this country for the children who benefit by family allowances. So my hon. friend is in company with these people, I do not say on all counts, but he is advocating a measure that they support.
Quit smearing me; that is what that is.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not smear anybody; I can argue without smearing anyone.
That is what you are doing right now.
If my hon. friend thinks I have smeared him I wish he would rise in his place and say wherein I have done so.

My point of order is that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has deliberately tried to associate me with l'union des electeurs, and then quoted their attitude toward the defence budget to continue the suggestion that that is my attitude. The minister knows that is not my attitude or the attitude of any member of this group. The attempt to associate me with the attitude of l'union des electeurs was the reason I made the interjection I did.

Shake hands under the table.

Family Allowances Act

I was going to add that my hon. friend has some justification. I did not seek to say that he was implying that there should be no defence expenditure and I thought I had indicated that. If I did not, I indicate it now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister had better straighten it out.
What did my hon. friend say? I really want to know what my hon. friend said.
You implied that.

If I implied that my hon. friend was in favour of an increase in family allowances at the expense of our defence budget I withdraw that fully, because he said nothing of that character. But what he did was support a measure which would have the result of forcing me to say that we cannot do this. We could not double family allowances when we had a defence budget of $2 billion. That is what I am saying.
That is not the only argument in this connection. I think it is my duty to indicate that we do not really know what my hon. friend is proposing. He has not said whether he wants family allowances increased by 50 cents, by one dollar, by two dollars or doubled. I do not know, but I am assuming that he wants them increased in some way. There is surely an obligation on him, or on any hon. member who makes a proposal in this house, to indicate whether he wants family allowances doubled or simply increased by 60 per cent as he proposed a number of years ago. I cannot read my hon. friend's mind. I shall have to assume that he has something definite in mind.
In December, 1954, the average family allowance in Canada worked out at $6.04 per child. On that basis the annual cost of family allowances is $369,986,000, which is a great deal of money. If the average family allowance were increased by $1, that is, increased to $7.04, the annual cost would be $431,244,000. If the increase were $2 the total payment would reach almost $500,000,000. If the allowance were doubled, which is the proposal of the organization known as Tunion des electeurs, to an average of $12.08 per child, the total cost of family allowances would be nearly three-quarters of a billion dollars-precisely $738,968,000.
Is there any hon. gentleman in this house who will rise in his place and say he agrees that this is a responsible proposal at a time when we are engaged heavily in the building up of our defences, when we are engaged in a responsible expansion of social measures? If we had accepted my hon. friend's proposal

a number of years ago does any hon. member think it would have been possible to have an old age security program that is costing Canada over $350,000,000 a year? If we had accepted my hon. friend's proposal last year would we have been able to bring in the disability allowances program last year? If we had accepted my hon. friend's proposal would we have been able to bring in legislation to help the blind, or to bring in a national health program? My hon. friend nods yes. I say we could never have done these things if four years ago-
If war came tomorrow you would do 10 times as much.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My friend says if war came we would do 10 times as much. My hon. friend is right. If our freedom and our way of life were in jeopardy this nation and all the free peoples of the world, including my hon. friend, would want us to resist to the last.
The welfare of the people is in jeopardy now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows perfectly well that these things must be viewed in their proper context.
My friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-and I do not quarrel with this because I am generally able to handle myself when he puts a question to me-asks me about the possibilities of health insurance. He has an interest, as have all other hon. members, in doing something in co-operation with the provinces to provide a responsible system of care for the sick through a proper system of hospital and medical insurance. Assuming that the provinces take the initiative, as under our constitution they must, does he think for one minute that if we were to load up the family allowance program beyond all proportion having regard to other social measures, there would be any opportunity in the foreseeable future of doing those important things in the field of health? Of course not. What I have said applies not only to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre but to all other hon. members.
When my hon. friend today pointed out the desire of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to bring in a balanced budget this year, he might have mentioned the fact that the Department of National Health and Welfare was one of a minority group of departments of government whose expenditures this year were higher than they were last year. He did not tell the house that our family allowance payments this year will be $17J million

higher than they were last year. No. According to him this government is callous; some of the membership of this house are not interested in the children of this country. Mr. Speaker, I think every hon. member in this house recognizes the value of the family allowance and realizes its relationship to other obligations and other social measures, both those now existing and others we might from time to time have in mind.
I close what I have to say with this further observation. My hon. friend has taken his position today vaguely. As I said at the outset, there are many people in this country who take the opposite position, namely that Canada is spending too much money in the field of health and welfare. I have answered my hon. friend. I should like now to answer this latter group. We are not irresponsible in the expenditures we are making on federal account in the field of health and welfare. Our expenditures, which now are over $1,200 million, represent only one-half of 1 per cent more than we spent in these fields in 1938, in relation to the net national income or the national product. There has been no irresponsible administration of health and welfare measures in this country.
I do not say that we have done everything perfectly, but I do not like the suggestions made in certain newspapers in this country, especially certain financial journals, to the effect that the government has become irresponsible through its Minister of National Health and Welfare with respect to these expenditures in these important fields. I am convinced beyond any shadow of doubt that while at present there is no course open to the free world but to build up our defences so we can be strong enough to resist force if it should ever be used in wanton aggression from any quarter, I am satisfied that in the long run the kind of social and health measures we have introduced in this country in the last decade and a half, setting a pattern for what we will do in the future, will be one of our best bulwarks against dialectical materialism or communism as practised by those ruthless men in the Kremlin. I am sure of that.
We are not the authors of a welfare state. I deprecate the use of that word. It is used often by editorial writers in criticizing me and other members of the government. I even find that sinister phrase creeping into the recent book on Lloyd George written by Frank Owen. During the British prime minister's time no one in the United Kingdom or anywhere else ever used the words "welfare state". It is a term of recent vintage. If by welfare state you mean emphasis on welfare, then this government believes in the welfare state. But if the term welfare state means creating greater powers for the state
Family Allowances Act and curtailing the liberties of the ordinary human being, then this government does not believe in that kind of welfare state.
Mr. Speaker, this family allowance measure about which I have made a report today is a monument to the vision and the humanitarian qualities of the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. It is a measure that has now received the support of every political party in this country. As the minister responsible for the administration of this measure I can say that this country need not be ashamed of having adopted the Family Allowances Act.

Mr. Speaker, in the light of what has been said this afternoon in connection with this resolution introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia, I feel that I must take a few minutes of the time of the house in order to make a few things clear. My name was mentioned on one occasion and I felt that it was something of a challenge to me to say something and perhaps speak on this measure for the group I represent.
I should like to start by saying that we were glad when the family allowance scheme was introduced back in 1944, because for a good long time we had been promoting some such idea. I am not going to take the time of the house today to enter into any quarrel about where the idea originated. I will say in passing, however, that there must have been some relationship between the $25 a month proposal of Mr. Aberhart in Alberta, a gift of purchasing power to the people of the country, and the family allowances that were introduced as a gift of purchasing power by the late Mr. W. L. Mackenzie King. He could not quite match the $25, but he came close to it.
The fact is that this scheme was introduced for two purposes. The first was to give a certain measure of stability to the economy. I distinctly remember Mr. Mackenzie King saying so. He said that when the war was over and we had to absorb back into our economy the two million young people who were engaged in military operations, we would have to find some way of keeping the level of purchasing power high so as to provide a market for the greater production that would be brought into being as a consequence of taking those young people back into civil life. We agreed with him because for a long time that was exactly what we had argued.
The second reason Mr. Mackenzie King gave at the time was exactly the reason that was cited here this afternoon by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, with all it implied; it was to help our families have a decent standard of nutrition, schooling, medi-

Family Allowances Act cal care and all that sort of thing. Those things cannot be denied. We were glad, as I say, when we saw this form of national dividend introduced in this country.
I use that term advisedly. It is exactly a national dividend, because it is nothing but a gift of purchasing power every month to the children between certain ages in this country. I do not care what you call it. The point is that it is a gift of purchasing power. We felt that the two purposes cited by Mr. Mackenzie King were sound and good, and we therefore supported the idea and support it today. I wish to say, too, that over the 10 years during which family allowances have been operative in this country they have done a tremendous amount of good, and I commend the Liberal government for having introduced them. I do not want to take away from them any glory that is coming their way for having done so and having stood by their guns. I think we are all grateful for the fact that family allowances have, without any question, achieved the purposes for which they were introduced.
Having said that, I should like to pay a bit of attention to some of the things that have been said by some of the other speakers. I refer for the moment to my good friend the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). My genial friend always has a good time. I enjoy him. He keeps his good humour, and I like that. When he is speaking he never seems to exhibit any rancour; and, while his thrusts sometimes are pointed and they go home, at the same time I enjoy him very much. But this afternoon I think he did not make clear in his speech on family allowances the difference between the policies put forward by the Social Credit Association of Canada and the union of electors of Quebec. He said it is Social Credit policy that family allowances can be doubled, tripled, etc., without taxation. I have never made such a statement as that without making a qualification, and I do not think any member of the Social Credit Association of Canada has ever done so.
Let me make the matter clear. I am in thorough agreement with the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre when he says that under present financial policy the only way that you can increase family allowances is either to increase taxation or to pare down some of the other services, take the money saved and pay it in family allowances.
If my hon. friend will permit me, he is more honest than l'union des electeurs. I hope he will disassociate himself from them.

I want to make it very clear where we stand because it is important, when Social Credit and its policies are dis-

cussed in the house, that it be understood what it is that the Social Credit Association of Canada really does put forward. The Social Credit Association of Canada is a political action movement. Therefore we are in a responsible position where we must take a good, thorough look at everything we propose so we will not be bringing upon the Canadian people additional burdens of taxation which they cannot bear. That is the thing I want understood today.
I should like to see an increase in family allowances, certainly; and I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South when he says he is certain the day will come when there will be an increase. I think that time will come. I hasten to say right here that I can show one way whereby the allowances can be increased without increasing taxation or taking away from any other service. Perhaps I can show another later. If we concentrate our attention on putting cents back into the Canadian dollar to bring its purchasing value to what it formerly was in those days when we had a dollar that would buy a dollar's worth, then by that measure family allowances will certainly be increased.
Let me give some idea of what that would amount to. The Minister of National Health and Welfare cited some very interesting figures this afternoon. If I remember his figures correctly, he said that last year the average payment per child under family allowances was $72.88. That would pretty nearly agree with the figures I have compiled for the years since 1945. I think that is what last year's payment would indicate this year's would be. The $72.88 per child per year is in terms of 1954 dollars, but let me hasten to point out what has happened over the years. The real purchasing power of the $72.88 average per child per year would only be $39.60 when you realize that there has been an increase in the cost of living index to approximately 184 on the basis of the old index. Apply the index of 184 to the $72.88 and you get the real purchasing value today of $39.60.
That would indicate that there has been a confiscation of the purchasing power of the family allowances of the difference between $72.88 and $39.60, which amounts to $33.28 per child in a year. In other words, by allowing the purchasing value of the Canadian dollar to decline to its present position we have actually taken away from each child, based on this year's payments, $33.28 of purchasing power. When you translate that into terms of some commodity like milk, for example, which today has an average price throughout Canada of approximately 21-2 cents per quart, it means that we have denied every child in this country 157 quarts of milk in the year.

I think that was the basis of the argument used by the hon. member for Assiniboia. On the basis of that argument he is quite right. We have not kept the purchasing power of our dollar at or near the original level, and as a consequence the present level of family allowances is not adequate to do what it was originally designed to do. But there that argument has to stop. If we are going to increase family allowance payments, under present financial policy we have to do it either by taxation or by taking away from some of the other services.
Let me make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that at no time has the Social Credit Association of Canada ever proposed that we should decrease the appropriations for defence purposes for the purpose of paying social security. I think under present circumstances that would be a most irresponsible proposal to make, and we do not make it because we realize that we are living in days of danger, when it is essential that we be as strong as we possibly can. If we are going to negotiate for peaceful settlement of the world's problems we have to negotiate from strength, and we have to be in a position to defend ourselves against the dangers that beset us on ev*ry hand. Consequently we feel that the responsible position to take is to continue to make ourselves strong, and let us not reduce our appropriations for defence except to the extent that we possibly can reduce them by greater efficiency. Certainly I would never say that under present circumstances we should take the money for defence and pay it out in family allowances.
I am dissociating myself and my group from that proposal. I hope that is understood. Therefore when the hon. member for Temis-coUata says that we suggest increasing family allowances, or doubling or tripling them, without increased taxation, it is not this group that is making the suggestion. The hon. member for Temiscouata also took the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) to task for having said-
He thought he did.

Well, of course I suppose we are all subject to that limitation-in a speech in the House of Commons some months or years ago that it could be that machine production in this country would throw a great many men out of work. That of course has happened. My hon. friend knows it has happened. Let us take a look at the figures. He must know that largely through technical advances in machinery and better methods of production through machine use, hours of labour have been greatly reduced in the past few years. For instance, it was not very long
Family Allowances Act ago, and quite within my experience, when the work week was 60 hours. Today what is it? In most places it is 40 hours or 48 hours, not more than 48. In most places it is 40 hours, and I suppose the average would be somewhere around 44. What has made the difference? The introduction of machines, and certainly an increase in technology.
My hon. friend must also admit that even though that is the case we have not solved the problem of employment, because today what have we? There are 600,000 people out of work, even with the 40 or 44-hour week. He must admit that the hon. member for Lethbridge was on the right track when he said that the continued use of machines and advanced methods of production would inevitably throw a lot of people out of work. The question my hon. friend poses is, where is the increased purchasing power to come from to purchase all the goods which we are capable of producing in this country? That is what he was pointing out. My hon. friend, in his inimitable way, ridiculed it; but I am sure that is all the hon. member was trying to do.

He ridiculed himself,
really.

I think the hon. member for
Lethbridge was certainly on the right track.

If my hon. friend will permit me to interject, I referred to the description of that machine, not exactly of that machine but what that machine could do by way of making fruits, fish, shoes and so on available, in the first place. In the second place, I quoted the hon. member for Lethbridge as stating that two men could operate that famous machine and make a living for 98 per cent of mankind. That was what I did not understand.

I shall have to let the hon.
member for Temiscouata and the hon. member for Lethbridge get together on that matter. Each can tell me what he had in mind, and then I shall try to understand it.
Let us all hear it.

All the hon. member
needed to do was look down the street at the snow-clearing machinery, and he would understand what is happening.

If I may continue, I would say that certainly under the present financial policy it would be impossible and impracticable to attempt to load the Canadian people with an extra burden of taxation to increase family allowances at this time. I believe that is true; but that does not mean there is no way by which it could be accomplished. I believe there is. I feel that it may have its

Family Allowances Act limitations, but I am going to put it forward just the same. I feel it would be possible, if a new financial policy were introduced throughout the country, to increase family allowances without increasing taxation or paring down defence or any other necessary appropriations for the government.
I am quite certain it is possible, but I am not going to take the time of the house to put the proposal forward in detail. I will say this. If we discover this year 500,000 or 600,000 unemployed in our country who are unable to earn because they cannot find work, that must be very largely because of the accumulation of unsold goods, goods that cannot find a market. If the financial policy of the government were to make available to the consumers of this country, by means of a national dividend, the purchasing power with which they could buy the surplus goods and take them off the market, we could very soon increase employment and in fact do away with the problem of unemployment.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, it would have to be done very responsibly and very carefully. If the Bank of Canada were to advance to the government sufficient purchasing power to make up the deficiency that exists between the total price of goods available for sale and the effective purchasing power in the pockets of the consumers with which to buy the goods, then that amount could be distributed in the form of national dividends or family allowances, I do not care what you call it. This amount of purchasing power would then balance our economy and make it possible for us to quit worrying very much about unemployment.
If we were to do that under present circumstances, however, the Bank of Canada would have to declare an increase in the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks in order to prevent inflation. We realize that. But under the revised act they have the right to declare an increase in the cash reserve requirement. By that method they could prevent inflation. The amount of new purchasing power issued may not be sufficient to take care of the kind of increase in family allowances that the hon. member for Assini-boia had in mind. It may not be anything like the amount required to do what l'union des electeurs of Quebec suggest. We would have to limit the amount which could be issued to the exact deficiency of purchasing power between the price of goods offered for sale and the effective purchasing power in the pockets of the people with which to buy those goods. If that were one dollar, then that is all that could be safely issued without creating inflationary trends. If it were $2 million, that would be the limit. If it were $10 million, that would be the limit.
(Mr. Low.]
I certainly hold no brief for those people who take the view that you can go on issuing purchasing power indiscriminately, unrelated entirely to our production increases; not by any means. I hold the position, and I am speaking for my movement, that as the production of the country increases the purchasing power of the country will have to increase to keep pace with it, otherwise we will not be able to distribute the goods. If there were a 1 per cent increase in production, then you could safely increase the total purchasing power of your country by 1 per cent. It would have to be limited to that. I hope that makes the position clear.
Let me say in conclusion that we feel it would be possible, under a changed financial policy, to increase family allowances. We feel that a good case can be made for increasing family allowances without taxation. We do feel, however, that we must take into account the position of our taxpayers in this land, and not heap upon them any further burdens of taxation. At the same time we must be very careful to see to it that every policy we introduce in this country will have the effect of putting cents back into the Canadian dollar, by increasing the purchasing value of the Canadian dollar. When we do that certainly we are, by that means, increasing family allowances in proportion. Those are the things that we feel should be done.

I congratulate the hon. member for Assiniboia, for two reasons, Mr. Speaker. He made a good speech and he showed outstanding imagination. The result of his speech was to bring forth one of the finest deliveries we have heard from the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He has shown to us the foundation on which family allowances are built. I congratulate both hon. members on what one called forth and what the other measured up to, just in the usual way.
There are three reasons why I cannot yet support this resolution. I believe I know the homes in Fort William better than any man in this house, and almost as well as most people in that city. I have never yet heard the mother of a family say she is dissatisfied with family allowances; never once have I heard one say that she wanted more. But I have heard many of them say that it has been a great boon to them to get that cheque once a month.
Therefore I say that is one reason there is no call for an increase. Then, second, sometimes I visit the public schools and see how the children are dressed. I see the children not only in the public schools but in the high schools and technical schools, Protestant and

Roman Catholic. I see the school yards crowded with bicycles; and at this season of the year hundreds of the school children have been able to purchase their own skates. So why should more cash be paid to those homes by the dominion government? Surely that is a sound argument.
Then, when a young man has made up his mind to choose a partner for life, what does he do? If he is a real Canadian he will provide a nest. He will have more than a room in a rented suite. He will have something more than a cigarette lighter. That man will have a nest for her. Then when a wise Providence comes with a happy bundle from heaven, what does the father do? He goes to his young wife and he says, "Now we will have to measure up to our responsibility. I shall cut out cigarettes; I shall cut out light refreshments. I shall spend less money on myself." He does not say "Oh, we will get $5 for this child, and we will have more to spend." That is not the type of young Canadian I know.
Then let us suppose that his companion is a bachelor. He says, "I am not going to have a home of my own." He denies himself the great privilege and happiness of a home, but when the happy little bundle comes to the other house he is supposed to help his friend pay the cost.
Another reason I am not in favour of this resolution just now is that there are greater needs in Canada. As I have said before, veterans of the first war should have pensions at the age of 60 years, without a means test. Just the other day I met a friend of mine who said that his company was ordered into the trenches and told they would be there for only three or four days. However, they were there for 31 days, and the trench was never without a foot of water in it. The shells were coming over constantly. The lives of men in that position would be shortened by at least 10 years. This is an outstanding need; and I am going to fight for it, and it will have my support before I would be prepared to support an increase in family allowances.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare knows perfectly well that I have supported national health insurance, and we are going to see it in this country before we close our eyes in the long sleep. We are going to have a national health insurance scheme. We are not going to have it this year, but I expect it will come-and it will come before we have an increase in family allowances.
I am convinced there is no need at the present time for this increase because mothers
Family Allowances Act and fathers are not seeking it. The need is not pressing. There are other things far more urgent.
I thank hon. members for their courtesy in having listened to me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the attack made by the minister of national welfare upon my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia, and against this party as a whole, and despite what I shall say before taking my seat a few minutes from now, I wish in my first words to take the part of the Minister of National Health and Welfare in one respect, and I assure him it will be in one respect only.
I noted his complaint that certain newspapers in this country have referred to him as an irresponsible minister because he is spending so much money on health and welfare. and because he is trying to get more money for expenditure in that field. Far from any suggestion that the minister's efforts or those of any other person in that connection are irresponsible, I suggest they are highly responsible. I go further than that and say that in this time of uncertainty and tension in the world at large it is important not only that we look to our material and military defences, but that we concern ourselves with the strength of our people in every way; and not the least important of our concerns should be in the field of health and welfare. The minister is perfectly right in every effort he makes in this field. I suggest the same applies to others who likewise may be seeking to strengthen our position in the matter of health and welfare.
I said I was taking the part of the minister in only one respect. As for the rest of his speech, I certainly do not agree with the description applied to it by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). Once again the minister was trying to have it both ways. He wanted all the credit he could gather to himself and his party for family allowances and other social legislation, but he also wanted to take the position that at this time nothing more could be done. He wants to build a monument to Mackenzie King for family allowances, but he does not want to do anything to stop the crumbling of that monument that is taking place because of the effects of inflation on the value of family allowance cheques.
I suggest that if the Minister of National Health and Welfare wants to boast either justifiably or erroneously of what the Liberal party has done in the field of social welfare it would be far better to implement that boast by doing something to preserve the
1450	HOUSE OF
Family Allowances Act value of such social legislation as we now have, and by doing something to extend its provisions.
This afternoon the minister suggested that anyone who asked for an increase in family allowances was blocking the way to health insurance. He suggested that this gets in the way of doing something more in the field of old age pensions. The hon. member for Fort William suggested that it gets in the way of improving the position of the veterans. They all ask the question: If you spend the money on this, where will you get the money for other things? The first reply is that the government is not making any serious attempt to find money for these other things. The second reply is that if the government had done something about unemployment in the past two or three years we would have had in this country during that period of time more than sufficient extra wealth to take care of all the things we are asking with respect to health insurance, old age pensions and increased family allowances.
Far from the proposal by my seatmate, the hon. member for Assiniboia, being irresponsible, I suggest his proposal, along with our other proposals regarding old age pensions and health insurance, is highly responsible. Indeed these things are related to the need for increased strength on the part of the people of this country at this very time.
In part of his speech with which I shall not deal in detail now, the Minister of National Health and Welfare this afternoon tried to link my seatmate with another organization. That matter was straightened out, I believe, when my colleague the hon. member for Assiniboia rose on a question of privilege. I suggest that if the Minister of National Health and Welfare wanted to find out what other organizations might be advancing, along the lines of the proposal before us this afternoon, he should have looked at the proposal of the Canadian Congress of Labour, than which there is no more responsible body in Canada, which has proposed that there should be an increase in family allowances to the extent of $2 in each category.
The hon. member recommended doubling the family allowances.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Instead, the minister tried to make that association between my hon. friend and a group with which none of us in this house has any connection. The minister is also using the phrase about the doubling of family allowances. That is one of his complaints. On the other hand, he complains that my colleague's motion is vague in that it asks just for an increase in the amount, without specifying the extent to


which he wants that increase to be made. Which way does the minister want it? A few days ago another motion was before the house asking for the doubling of a certain payment because of the increased cost of living, or the decrease in the value of the dollar. In a speech the other night, which was very much like the speech made this afternoon by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the Minister of Agriculture-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He made a much better speech.
You are right there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I shall let the ministers fight that out between themselves. The Minister of Agriculture suggested that if, instead of asking that the amount be doubled, the motion had just asked for an increase, he could have considered it. Now this afternoon we get a motion which avoids what the Minister of Agriculture did not like. It just asks for an increase, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare says he cannot consider it because it does not specify precisely what my hon. friend wants. There you have it; the government wants things both ways. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take any undue time because I would like to see this resolution come to a vote, but I do feel there are just one or two other things I should say while I am on my feet. First of all, this is something I have intended to do every year when this debate has been up, because inevitably this house seems to get to the question of who started the campaign for family allowances in this country. Last year, as a matter of fact, after the debate was over I had a letter from a friend of many of us in this house, the late A. A. Heaps, written just before he died, who reminded me that 40 years ago he was a member of a delegation that waited on the provincial government of Manitoba, requesting legislation of this kind. Hon. members know, too, of the speeches that were made by various members in this house, particularly the late Mr. Heaps, and the late J. S. Woodsworth, supported by some others on the other side, back in the 1920's, calling for legislation of this kind.
However, Mr. Speaker, I hold in my hand a document which was the first of its kind in this country. This was the first time that a national political party in Canada wrote family allowances specifically into its national platform. This is the platform of the C.C.F., as adopted at the national convention held in Toronto in 1942. This document was issued under date of July 29 of that year. 1 find in this document a paragraph entitled "Social Justice". I read one or two sentences:
The first need, in war as in peace, is to safeguard the welfare of the Canadian family.

Under that, the C.C.F. proposed at that time that we should have the following measures: a floor below which no person's income should be allowed to fall; increased old age pensions starting at 60; and pensions for unemployables. In other words we asked then for the disability pension that we finally have achieved. I read on: national health insurance and family allowances. I suggest, therefore, that until some other national political party can produce a document earlier than 1942, with a specific proposal for family allowances in it, that is the record as to where the parties of this country stand on this question.
The next year, 1943, the Marsh report, which was produced under the direction of the late Prime Minister King, proposed family allowances, and in 1944 the legislation was introduced in this house and became law in 1945.
You are not a national party; you are a splinter party.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Unfortunately a slight bit of evidence has been given today of what the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek says, namely that we sometimes have a slight splinter, in that one member of this party has expressed his opposition to the resolution that is now before the house. I feel it is only fair to this party, and to all who are interested in keeping the record straight, that it should be made clear to this house that the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, who has exercised the privilege that is his of speaking for himself, was doing just that, and that he was speaking only for himself when he said he was against this proposal.
My colleague the hon. member for Assini-boia placed this resolution on the order paper not only on his own behalf but on behalf of this C.C.F. group. But I go further. I wish to place on the record another statement from a C.C.F. national convention. At this time I hold in my hand a copy of the record of our twelfth national convention which was held in 1952, also in the city of Toronto, at which time we passed a rather lengthy resolution on all phases of social security. I shall not read it all, but under the heading "Social Security" I quote this:
(e) an Increase in family allowances to compensate for the increase in the cost of living since they were first established, and the continuance of family allowance payments for children from 16 to 21, as long as they remain at school or college.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, what everyone knows is quite clear. The resolution that is before the house at the present time in the name of the hon. member for Assiniboia
Family Allowances Act clearly represents the position of this C.C.F. party.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the resolution. Since my colleague the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Enfield) also wishes to say something, I shall give him the opportunity shortly.
First of all I should like to agree with the hon. member for Fort William, who wants a health insurance plan. He thinks that is more important at the present time than an increase in family allowances, but I shall deal with that in just a moment.
At the outset I should like to say that I believe the success of this government is due to the balance they hold between private and public enterprise. That is fundamental, because a government which believes in private enterprise has to take into consideration the public interest. In that regard it is paramount that certain public enterprises should be encouraged, and that has been the case. Because of this we have a very comprehensive social security plan in this country. We have unemployment insurance; we have family allowances; we have old age pensions, and we have other kinds of social legislation.
In my own riding I find that most of the people are interested in health insurance. I have had no requests that family allowances should be increased, but I have had several inquiries as to when we were going to get a national health plan. I feel that the Minister of National Health and Welfare should be warmly congratulated on the fine program he has instituted in this country in the interests of the people.
I submit that at the present time there are many reasons why family allowances cannot be increased substantially. For example, we must remember that many new expenditures are being made this year in the field of social security. We have an increase in the war veterans allowance. Last night the Minister of Veterans Affairs stated that this government was increasing the allowance to single pensioners from $50 to $60 and for married pensioners from $90 to $108, and that the permissible ceilings are also being raised. Again, we have legislation having to do with disabled persons, and an increase in unemployment insurance. In other words, Mr. Speaker, there are continual increases in social security benefits in this country.
It seems to me that if we are to have these increases we cannot also increase the family allowances at the present time. I have no hesitation in saying that I shall support vigorously any social security measure in this country, but the hon. member for Assini-
1452	HOUSE OF
Family Allowances Act boia always gives me the impression that he represents the repository of all wisdom. If we are to have increased expenditures on social security I should like to see more money spent on bringing in a national health insurance plan and on bursaries for needy university students in conformity with the resolution that I have on the order paper at the present time. Second, I would be forced to vote against this resolution moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I wish to say that I will always support family allowances and that I think it is the Liberal government who will set the example in reform in this country.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, some of the arguments advanced in opposing this resolution remind me a great deal of the arguments we had during the thirties. It was assumed then that there really was not very much we could do about having poverty in the midst of plenty. Last night I was reading a book by Robert Sherwood dealing with Roosevelt and Hopkins. While this book dealt primarily with the war period, I think more people should read about the imaginative way in which Roosevelt and his associates dealt with a very real economic problem in the United States 20 years ago. In reply to a question asked by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) the minister readily admitted that if war should break out Canada would have no trouble in raising 10 times the amount proposed to increase family allowances.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I did not say we would have no trouble; I said that Canadians generally would do everything possible to preserve their way of life.

If we should have the misfortune to have a third world war, and assuming that it could go on for four years, I am sure events would prove that Canada could raise enormous sums.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) raised two relevant questions. He mentioned the responsibility to old age pensioners and to those who are getting war veterans allowances. I think we cannot at this time justify our shabby treatment of the people getting war veterans allowances and of our old age pensioners by the argument that the present scale of payments for family allowances is stretching our economy.
The hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out that if people now unemployed were given a chance to do productive work, a very


large amount of new wealth would be created. Yesterday someone mentioned that there are 600,000 in the ranks of the unemployed at the moment. It is estimated that on the average every person who works creates at least $8 worth of new wealth in return for a day's work. That is a total of $4,800,000 a day that the people of Canada are losing by condemning 600,000 of our fellow Canadians to continued unemployment, or a total of $1,440 million a year of new wealth which would be available if we gave these unemployed a chance to work. That is seven times the increase of $200 million mentioned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare over the present amount of $384 million.
I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare made his unfortunate reference to the premier of Saskatchewan. If he would like to have the unanimous consent of the house to have that section expunged from the record I am sure we would give it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Are you asking me a question?

No, but I am suggesting that if at six o'clock the minister asks for unanimous consent we should give it. The Minister of National Health and Welfare and the premier of Saskatchewan came here together in 1935 as bright young men.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We are still bright young men.

I am sure that while the premier of Saskatchewan was minister of health the Minister of National Health and Welfare found there was no other minister of health in Canada who gave more complete co-operation. I think on reflection he will ask that that reference be withdrawn.
When the debate started I was reading the New York Times, and I noticed that they are proposing in Washington to increase the pay of members of congress from $15,000 to $25,000 a year. The judges are having their salaries increased from $25,000 to $35,000, and the salaries of the vice-president and the Speaker are being increased from $40,000 to $45,000. Is it not strange that increases of this sort never place any strain on the national economy? When we considered increases for the members of this house and of the Senate a year ago, very few, if any, hon. members raised any question about what those increases would do to the economy of Canada.
I submit that the proposal of the hon. member for Assiniboia is sound. Every political party is for family allowances. If it was a sound principle in 1944 or 1945 to earmark 2 per cent of our gross national product for family allowances, I submit that it is a sound policy in 1954. The proposal made by the

hon. member for Assiniboia to increase this amount would really have a beneficial effect upon our economy. Those people who are unfortunate in that they do not receive enough to have to pay income tax are placed in a most difficult position in that their incomes are not sufficient to provide enough food, clothing and shelter for their families. Here is one simple step that can be taken by the federal parliament to make it possible for every Canadian family to have additional purchasing power.
I agree with those who have stated that in the final analysis the wealth of Canada is produced by all the people of Canada and that there is a limit to the amounts that can be spent by the provincial, federal and municipal authorities. But I submit that the people in the lower income brackets are not receiving a sufficient share of the national income. If we will take steps to see that the unemployment problem is solved and that our agricultural producers are given a fair share of the national income, then the federal government will have no problem in meeting the commitment suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

Mr. Speaker, the humorous reference of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) to the wonderful Social Credit machine is perhaps not as far wide of the mark as it might at first appear to be, because the government have their own version of this wonderful machine, and its name is inflation. It may be necessary in order to have a social security program to have a policy of inflation, but I suggest that the government should tell the people this quite frankly. It is perfectly obvious that a large portion of the funds necessary to finance the social security program of the government are obtained in this way, and my suggestion is that the public of this country be informed of that fact.

Mr. Speaker, I think we can all agree that it would be nice to adopt the role of a big spender whenever we are faced with resolutions of this nature, but since the institution of the family allowance scheme we have increased our spending on social security by a tremendous amount. Over the years we have instituted an unemployment insurance program; a very generous program for veterans of the second world war by means of war veterans allowances; we have our vocational training and health grants. It is very pleasant to be the author, to be in power and to have an opportunity to put into effect these most popular measures. However, fortunately, the principle on which the financial
Family Allowances Act measures of our form of government are based is that the person who spends the money is the one who is responsible for raising it. I thought the house might be interested in an article which appeared in the Financial Post which highlights this point. It is dated February 13, 1954 and is entitled "It All Depends Where They Sit", and reads in part as follows:
Practical experience is a wonderful teacher. Out in Saskatchewan the other day provincial treasurer Fines of the C.C.F. government in that province offered this advice in a provincial hook-up:-
I presume it was a radio hook-up.
-"We must not increase our social services, health services and education services to a level beyond which we cannot maintain them."
It is too bad that federal members of the same party at Ottawa do not heed that very sound advice. Apparently they were not listening. Instead they have been suggesting that the senior government should step up its family allowances by 60 per cent, which would have added close to $200 million a year to the tax bill of Canada. As the Regina Leader-Post observes:
"It probably is too much to ask Ottawa C.C.F.'ers to heed the sound and admirable words of their own Mr. Fines so that they would desist from absurd and extravagant demands which patently are beyond the ability or willingness of the people of Canada to carry along with present defence expenditures. The Ottawa C.C.F.'ers know as well as anyone that their proposals are impractical. They are advanced for the sole purpose of winning friends and votes from among those who may favour family allowance increases, and extensions of the other social welfare and health services, without stopping to count up the cost."
It would appear that there is no great degree of unanimity among people of socialist thought on the soundness of the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The government is in the position, therefore, of having to take the responsibility of collecting the money it pays out in such social services.
Did you write his speech?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No.

I should perhaps mention to the hon. member for Assiniboia that I do not have anyone write my speeches for me. Like some other hon. members, I found his discussion extremely thought-provoking. Along with the hon. member for Fort William I wish to thank him for instigating such an excellent discourse on social measures by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
You have three minutes to go.

I think we all learned a great deal from it. I must say also that I found of interest the speech made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). It has been stated that raising money is a good thing. We are forced at all times to remember that the money we collect represents trust funds in
1454	HOUSE OF
Family Allowances Act our hands held on behalf of the people, and that we must take great care of it. We are forced to extract from the public the money that we spend which is never a popular thing to do. On both counts our position demands extreme caution. We could tax beyond the productive capacity of the country or the nation. We could hence ruin incentive and cripple enterprise. On the other hand we could expand beyond the limit of our resources, go into debt and thus ruin confidence in our financial position and in the Canadian dollar.
I mention this consideration because I feel that we must examine measures such as the one introduced by the hon. member for Assiniboia in this context. I think the public have a tendency to examine social welfare measures purely from the humanitarian aspect. When they see something that is going to help families they say, "That is fine; it will help families". Then if there is something to help the veterans they say, "That is fine; it is good for the veterans". But I do not think the tendency is to look at the general effect of such measures on the economics of the country, or at the general effect in the realm of the fiscal policy of the government with which we are so greatly concerned in connection with every resolution of this nature with which we are faced concerning the spending of money or the raising of money.
It is natural for the public to look at the matter in that way. In so far as we have money to distribute, the humanitarian view decides to whom we are going to give it and in what manner. However, I respectfully submit that the humanitarian view is always subordinate to the economic consideration.
The hon. member for Assiniboia gave lip service to this argument when he argued that increasing the allowance might have the effect of increasing business activity and hence increasing government revenues. But if we are going to look at that argument-and I submit it is a good argument to look at-it opens up a whole new field of speculation.
There are 58 seconds left.
I thank the hon. member.
Thirty seconds.

Suppose we were in a position to increase government expenditures. We must ask ourselves the question, is the increase in family allowance the best way of producing the desired effect, or perhaps the effect that the hon. member for Assiniboia wants? Frankly, I can think of many alternative courses that we should at least study before we blindly commit ourselves to the course suggested by the hon. member. For example, perhaps the public would rather spend their own money. By that I mean if we wish to distribute further wealth over a wide cross-section of the public, we should consider leaving more spending power in their hands perhaps by means of reduction in the income tax at the lower level, rather than collecting more money by a scheme such as this, redistributing it, setting up all the complicated machinery to do so and then charging further income tax on the money so distributed.
I leave these matters for the consideration of the house. As it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I move that the debate be adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Enfield the debate was adjourned.
